slides.title: Fire Safety
slides.description:
Never use containers without lids or glass bottles for flammable liquid storage.

Keep flammable liquids and paints in closed, properly marked lockers and storage cabinets, where available.

Do not place or store flammable liquids, paints, etc., near sparks, heat or open flames.

Keep lids closed on solvent-based, parts-washing sinks when not in use.

Secure compressed oxygen and cylinders. Keep cylinders capped and stored away from heat, flames and sparks.

Never use oxygen from cylinders to blow away dirt, etc. Oxygen causes a highly flammable condition. Never refer to oxygen as “Air”

Properly dispose of paper cartons. Cardboard and paper could catch fire or smolder, if exposed to sparks, gasoline, etc.

Use only Underwriter Laboratory/Factory Mutual-approved safety cans with flame arresters and self-closing lids for storage of gasoline.

Don’t throw hot auto parts into a container of ignitable or flammable materials.

slides.title: Fire Extinguishers
slides.description:
Be sure you know the types of fires and extinguishers. There are four different types of fires: Class A, B, C and D. Fires can occur in a combination of these types.

Class A Fires (Ordinary Combustibles)Class A fires usually occur in materials such as: paper, cloth, wood or rubbish. A quenching-type extinguisher agent is needed for a Class A fire.

Class B Fires (Flammable Liquids)Class B fires in the vehicle/equipment maintenance facility usually involve: thinners, oils, gasoline, grease, paint or chemicals. Water must not be used on this type of fire because it will cause the fire to spread. Use a dry chemical B-type, C-type, ABC-type or carbon dioxide (CO₂)-type extinguisher on this type fire.

Class C Fires (Electrical Equipment)Class C fires involve energized electrical equipment such as an air-compressor motor or fuse box. Never use water-type extinguisher on electrical equipment; use a CO₂ extinguisher. BC – or ABC-type extinguishers may also be used on electrical fires .

Class D Fires (Combustible Metals) This type of fire involves the burning of materials that contain zirconium, lithium, magnesium, titanium or sodium. Class D fires are very rare in vehicle/equipment maintenance shops.

Fire extinguishers are to be charged and kept clean at all times, inspected annually and tagged with inspection dates.

CO₂ extinguishers generate an extremely cold gas (well below zero degrees) that can cause skin burns. Use caution when using this type of extinguisher.

slides.title: Using a Fire Extinguisher
slides.description:
Using a Fire Extinguisher,

Utilize the P.A.S.S system to remember how to use properly

Pull the Pinat the top of the extinguisher. The pin releases a locking mechanism and will allow you to discharge the extinguisher.

Aim at the base of the fire, not the flames. This is important - in order to put out the fire, you must extinguish the fuel.

Squeeze the lever slowly. This will release the extinguishing agent in the extinguisher. If the handle is released, the discharge will stop.

Sweep from side to side. Using a sweeping motion, move the fire extinguisher back and forth until the fire is completely out. Operate the extinguisher from a safe distance, several feet away, and then move towards the fire once it starts to diminish. Be sure to read the instructions on your fire extinguisher - different fire extinguishers recommend operating them from different distances. Remember: Aim at the base of the fire, not at the flames!!!!

slides.title: In the event you catch fire
slides.description: Reviewing the diagram to the right, observe how you should react if any part of your body catches fire. You should always follow the Stop Drop and Roll method.
